I think Conway's law applies. In an ideal situation your code mimics your organisational structure. The places where you let an agent do its thing is bound by the (implicit) interface your prompt creates. In an ideal situation this interface is a simple isolated thing in your application. If you just let it do its thing, expect a monolith. You shouldn't rely on it coming up with interfaces that mesh well with what you had in mind, and each of those interfaces represents a decision that it took, restricting future iterations of the code. There's a general trick which combines the time complexities. In the case of a sorted list, it's keeping a sorted list, along with a growing small unsorted list that you will query or sort when needed. This works for kernel timer trees, database storage, and indexes. Keep your "fixed" data up to some checkpoint in an efficient form, and your "new" data since the checkpoint in a faster-updating, slower-querying form. When doing queries, read both and merge, and maybe sort parts of the new data on demand. The new data will be slower to query, but it should also be smaller. At carefully chosen times, transfer data from the new form to the "fixed" form, either with an incremental update if you can, or by rewriting the fixed form entirely. It doesn't have to stop at two layers, and shouldn't if the fixed form is large, or if you want unlimited scale. Choosing the right times and how much to update (the whole key range, intervals, predicate subsets, ertc) is an interesting algorithm design problem. When you get it just right, you can get excellent performance in fast-queryable compression and continuous fast-updates at the same time. (I'm building a database engine that does this in my spare time.)

I can recommend an app called Libation. It downloads and decrypts your audible books into plain m4b or mp3. Then you can play them on any device using any player except the audible app. I've been using an android app called Voice. The author has recently done a bunch of rapid ai-fuelled not-all-great updates, but even so it's still a good simple working book player app with no ads and even available from fdroid not just google play. It's annoying having to find your own way to get the books onto your phone but it's even more annoying having books you paid for disappear. A few years ago I discovered several books I got years ago that don't exist any more. I complained and did actually get replacement book credits for some of them, which is something but I still don't have the books I wanted because they no longer exist. After that I don't allow any chance any more. I still buy books from Audible simply because for a lot of books there is no other choice. But I just immediately download them with Libation and copy them to a nas and my phone. Whatever Amazon does after that I don't care any more except as just collecting more examples as evidence that they do that. I could just continue to use the official app for the convenience and just download the archive copies seperately, but I actually like using a generic player app instead of the Audible app, and this way I can never forget to go back and archive them. There is also an app called OpenAudible but F that guy. He took gpl code and made a commercial app and stopped releasing the source. I did pay for that app and also donated to libation not to mention the countless Audible books since about y2k, so it's not about demanding stuff for free. The website says one-time license, but that's only true by a technicality. If you want the current version you have to keep paying for updates once a year. Paying for ongoing updates is not unreasonable but but writing "one-time license" when all that actually means is you can keep using an old version forever, that is somehow skeezy. And there is just something about putting a lock on your app whos whole purpose is actually just to break someone else's lock! The best would be to stop rewarding Amazon with sales but that is not realistic. There have been a few different competing services over the years but they've all eventually failed and gone away. AmblingBooks was awesome. They had an excellent player app that also played arbitrary other files not just their own, the books were downloadable and not encrypted. There was a short lived one called WeRead4You for a while that had unencrypted downloads. Currently I think the best competitor is Downpour but they have a fraction of the library and their prices went up and they generally cost a lot more than Audible now. I still try to use them when I can but it hasn't been much in the last few years. Anyway, Libation.

Alarm circuits are dedicated from point-to-point, not switched on demand using the PSTN, exactly so that a failure of telco switching equipment, remote as that possibility is, will not prevent an alarm from ringing on the other end. I don't like this framing. For a given model, the best harness depends on the problem. As models become increasingly capable, the harness appears to matter more than the model. This is perhaps controversial but allow me to explain. Most of my problems are in a single domain, using specific tools and programming languages. I give whatever model de jour the specific tools it needs to solve the problem. I don't let it execute arbitrary scripts or programs (though it can, if it really tries). I give it a restricted number of calls and I feed that information back into it (budget). I let it farm out work to other models, using the same harness. I give everything a budget, which is tracked and enforced, but it's not real, and refills at different times. This bespoke, specialized harness absolutely smokes any other mainstream harness for these tasks. Significantly faster, cheaper, more correct. But I can't build a mobile app with this harness, or make a movie. These tests are doing the same thing. They measure a handful of scenarios. I can't easily tell if those map to my needs or not. In my experience, very few of them do. Can these general purpose harnesses solve my problems? Yes, if I'm willing to let the model churn for a long time and burn a lot of tokens. But that doesn't feel like a sustainable practice. Maybe I'm too early, maybe it's premature to optimize the harness this way, but I'm spending fewer tokens than my peers and getting a lot more done, and that matters.
